name: Omar Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, government or unions, and your answers are confidential. Tell me about a usual shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Omar Abbott, 43, and I’m the one still learning linework after getting a vocational certificate. At the electricity company I load the truck, check the permit with the crew and help replace damaged conductors or fittings. The pay is high for this trade because I take awkward shifts, though I’m still junior and make the senior worker check my knots. I like finding the fault after a whole street has been staring at dark windows.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does work fit around home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Jo and I have two children at school and a mortgage, so a callout means a quick calendar message. We have more than six months of expenses saved and other utilities close enough to apply to. I use AI every day to quiz myself on diagrams and turn my notes into practice questions; I never treat its answer as clearance to touch a wire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a faster fault report is fine, but the actual line still has to be repaired. I’d show the apprentices my little practice quiz, then tell them to check every answer against the manual. A prompt cannot sign the permit for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be glad the learning curve has not suddenly moved again. My experience is the weak spot, not my willingness to try a tool, and the senior crew notices when I ask the same question twice. The savings mean I can keep earning my standing without chasing a higher title tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tonight I’d keep using my AI quiz for twenty minutes after the children go to bed, and I’d take it to a senior worker when an answer looks odd. In the first year I’d keep the same shift pattern and write down the faults I’ve actually repaired. I wouldn’t spend household money on a new system just to seem keen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. There is room to learn the craft without a new deadline over my shoulder. I still feel embarrassed when I need a second demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can you give me a time the quiz misled you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week the quiz said an old fitting had a different name from the one in our manual. I took both words to the truck, and the senior worker showed me the part in his hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change what you save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jo and I keep the emergency money in its own account. We are not adding to it because of a quicker report; we already have a cushion and the mortgage transfer is set.

say: I would welcome **faster reports** while reminding trainees that a person still signs the electrical permit.
I would share my **practice quiz** with apprentices and check its answers against the manual.
think: I need more **field experience**, even if the technology stops changing.
Our **six-month cushion** lets me keep learning without chasing a new title immediately.
do: Use the **AI quiz** for twenty minutes after the children sleep.
Keep the same **shift pattern** and record faults repaired during the first year.
feel: Calm about the slow pace, with occasional **embarrassment** when I need another demonstration.
S0.quote: A prompt cannot sign the permit for us.
fieldNote: Omar already uses AI as a **daily study aid**, yet his account of the mistaken fitting name shows manual checking.
He treats the plateau as a chance to gain **craft experience**, supported by strong savings and available shifts.

steps.text: Use the AI quiz after the children go to bed
Keep taking the same linework shifts this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my crew that the booking office will get faster and our repair tickets may look different. I’d ask for a field worker to test the new schedule before it becomes a target. If a computer counts a five-minute drive across a flooded bridge, someone ought to correct it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the office will lose roles before we do, and our foreman may push more tickets into each shift. That could cut overtime even while the base job stays; overtime is part of why our pay is good. I’m willing to use the software, but I don’t want my interest in it mistaken for consent to rush a live job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d volunteer for a supervised trial of the dispatch screen and keep a log of travel and repair times. I’d bring that log to the crew safety meeting and ask our union rep to press for a limit on tickets per shift. In the first year I’d revise my own fault notes using the new system, while still taking regular callouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I want the tool to cut useless driving, yet I know an attractive chart can hide a missing person on the crew. My own income looks fairly steady unless overtime disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of a ticket would the schedule miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d count from the time we reach the locked gate, not from when the vehicle stops on the map. Opening the site and testing it are work, even if software sees a blank square.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jo about money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would explain to Jo that a smaller overtime line is possible, not a lost job I can prove. We could keep paying the mortgage without the extra shifts, but weekend plans would get plainer.

say: I would ask a **field worker** to test automated dispatch before it sets the crew’s targets.
I would correct **travel estimates** that ignore blocked access or site checks.
think: I expect **office roles** to shrink before line repair jobs.
My **overtime pay** could shrink if management packs more tickets into each shift.
do: Volunteer for a supervised **dispatch trial** and log actual repair times.
Bring the **ticket log** to our safety meeting and seek union support for a shift limit.
Keep taking **callouts** while updating my fault notes from the new system.
feel: Uneasy about **overtime**, though I can see genuine value in less wasted driving.
S1.quote: Opening the site and testing it are work, even if software sees a blank square.
fieldNote: He wants to test dispatch **from the truck**, not merely receive its targets; his technology interest includes a measured challenge.
His pay relies partly on **overtime**, making a smaller schedule a credible household income risk despite strong savings.

steps.text: Trial dispatch software and log real repair times
Bring the ticket log to the union safety meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the thinking system coming in 2028 is one problem and the hands-on robots around 2031 are another. The company should give crews a real list of tasks and dates rather than calling everything automatic. I’d also ask who signs off a robot after a storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 45 I should still be on the truck while the office changes, but by 48 a capable repair robot could take the jobs I’m finally good at. I might be kept to oversee odd faults, or I might be the junior name crossed off a crew list. Our savings buy time, and nearby utilities give us choices, but neither guarantees the same pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d ask the training office for a funded place in substation testing and request the syllabus, then keep practising line repairs. In 2029 I’d apply for an internal testing post if one exists and keep taking paid field shifts. If robots reduce crews in 2031, I’d apply to neighbouring utilities for testing or repair work and cut the family holiday before using emergency savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can make applications, but I can’t manufacture vacancies. I would hate having finally earned the crew’s trust just as the work changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the new certificate protect you from robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want to know whether the testing role is hands-on too, because a robot might eventually take that as well. A certificate is only useful if it opens a real job for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our children that I’m training for another job at the electricity company, not that the house is at risk tomorrow. Jo and I would look at the mortgage together after I knew what the roster actually said.

say: I would distinguish **2028 thinking AI** from capable repair robots expected around 2031.
I would ask who must **sign off** a robot sent to a storm-damaged line.
think: I expect paid **field shifts** through the first change, but my junior place could be at risk after 2031.
Our **savings and nearby utilities** offer choices without guaranteeing my present wage.
do: Request a **funded testing place** and syllabus this month.
Apply for an internal **testing post** in 2029 while continuing line shifts.
Apply to nearby utilities and cut the **holiday** if robots reduce crews in 2031.
feel: Anxious that my **newly earned skill** might lose value just as the crew begins trusting me.
S2.quote: A certificate is only useful if it opens a real job for a while.
fieldNote: He separates an **office change in 2028** from the later physical repair risk, and expects to stay paid between them.
Unlike a broad promise to retrain, he asks for a **syllabus and vacancies**, then names local employers as a fallback.

steps.text: Request a funded substation testing course this month
Keep taking paid field shifts through 2029
Apply for internal testing and nearby utility posts
Cut the family holiday if 2031 field shifts fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the company to let lineworkers test the field robots before 2034, with the results shared across crews. Thinking AI in 2031 may rewrite plans, but I’ll still be climbing and repairing until physical machines actually work. A public failure log would help more than a glossy launch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 in 2031 I could have solid craft skills, despite being a beginner today. At 51 when the robots arrive, I’d still need a wage, because the children will be older but the mortgage does not vanish. I could use the warning to become the person who checks how those machines work in a real storm, but I’m not counting on that post existing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d ask the union and training office for a paid trial route into inspection work, and I’d keep photos of unusual faults with the company’s permission. I’d train on approved robot controls if a supervised course opens. In 2032 I’d apply for inspection vacancies and keep earning on the line; in 2034 I’d compare outside repair jobs if our shifts fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy now, because five years is usable time. I would be more anxious once the machines are actually taking callouts. I like testing things, but a clever test job can disappear after the trial is over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the inspection route credible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the trial manager whether inspection is a permanent rostered position and how many places exist. I’d also want the right to stop a robot if its camera cannot show a broken strand clearly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for a robot-testing job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I wouldn’t move the family for a trial contract. The children have a school here, and there are several utilities close enough to try first.

say: I would seek a **shared failure log** from field robot trials before the 2034 rollout.
I would remind crews that **2031 plans** change before robots can repair lines.
think: I could gain strong **craft skills** before the physical change, yet still need paid work at 51.
A temporary **trial post** would not automatically support our mortgage.
do: Seek a **paid inspection route** from the training office and union now.
Train on approved **robot controls** if a supervised course opens.
Apply for **inspection vacancies** in 2032 while continuing linework and comparing local repair jobs in 2034.
feel: Uneasy with usable **preparation time**, but wary of a test job that ends after the trial.
S3.quote: A public failure log would help more than a glossy launch.
fieldNote: Omar sees robot trials as a possible **inspection path**, then asks whether the position would survive a demonstration period.
He keeps the **family’s school** and mortgage in view, preferring local utility vacancies to a trial contract elsewhere.

steps.text: Ask the union for a paid inspection route
Train on approved robot controls if a supervised course opens
Apply for local inspection vacancies in 2032
Keep earning on line crews during the transition

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the younger crew members that ten years is worth using, not spending on rumours. Thinking AI comes in 2036 and robots able to do our field work around 2039. I’d want the electricity company to show us its workforce plan every year, in plain numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I may still be on the line, and at 56 I might prefer fewer night callouts. By then our children will be grown, so the school pickup problem is gone, but I have not checked what our retirement income would be. I’d rather make a choice with the mortgage mostly dealt with than discover a machine has chosen for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d request a retirement projection, then sit with Jo to compare it with the mortgage schedule. Over the decade I’d keep taking paid field work and look for a funded inspection qualification that lets me move toward daytime shifts. In 2037 I’d apply for a posted inspection role if the pay works; when field robots arrive in 2039 I’d decide whether to reduce nights from actual figures, not a birthday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm about the next few years, and a little restless about the longer horizon. Ten years gives us time to see what posts are real. I don’t need to pretend that 56 automatically means a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check in the retirement projection?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the benefits office for the monthly figure after tax, not just a large total on a statement. I might stay on nights if the daytime role paid too little to finish the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What information would the workforce plan need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the union to publish how many line jobs and inspection jobs were lost or added each year. A decade of numbers would let us plan better than a single demonstration day.

say: I would ask for **yearly workforce numbers** through the long transition.
I would mark **2036 and 2039** as separate dates for planning systems and field robots.
think: I may want fewer **night callouts** by 56, but I have not confirmed our retirement income.
Our children will be **grown**, while the mortgage and the actual daytime wage still matter.
do: Request a **retirement projection** and compare it with the mortgage now.
Continue paid **field work** while seeking funded inspection qualifications.
Apply for a **daytime inspection role** in 2037 if its pay meets our needs.
feel: Calm about the near years, with a **restless edge** about the longer field change.
S4.quote: I don’t need to pretend that 56 automatically means a pension.
fieldNote: His long plan begins with a **monthly retirement figure** and mortgage schedule rather than a guessed pension.
He remains interested in **field robots** but wants public workforce counts and a real paid role before reducing night shifts.

steps.text: Ask the union to publish yearly linework job counts
Keep taking paid field shifts through the decade
Seek funded inspection qualifications for daytime work
Apply for a daytime inspection post in 2037 if viable

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 is the hardest one for me. I can learn quickly, but I cannot turn two years into five years of experience on a line. A funded course tied to a posted job, a clear crew plan and the right to test robots before anyone relies on them would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the machine after a bad storm, when the drawings are wrong and the pole has moved. The line is never as tidy as the diagram. If I’m asked to trust a robot, I want the stop switch and a named person responsible for using it.

headlineQuote: The line is never as tidy as the diagram.
portrait: Omar is a **43-year-old junior lineworker** with a vocational certificate, high shift pay, two school-age children and a mortgage.
He uses **AI every day** for practice questions but checks technical answers against the manual and senior workers.
Strong savings and **local utilities** give him choices, though overtime and future crew numbers shape his income worries.
He volunteers to **test dispatch and robots**, asks for posted inspection roles and continues paid linework while learning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because two years cannot supply the field experience he hopes to build before robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a **funded course** linked to a posted job, a crew plan and supervised robot tests with clear responsibility.
